query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A tailored thermal annealing treatment that induces in‐situ precipitation of a fine, ductile secondary phase along grain boundaries will improve the mechanical integrity of the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high‐entropy alloy without significantly compromising its large caloric response under applied field and pressure cycling.
generation.material_initial_state: The untreated (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high‐entropy alloy exhibits a coarse microstructure with weak grain boundaries that lead to cracking, despite showing a robust caloric effect.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled annealing protocol at a temperature below the primary phase melting point, optimized to promote uniform in‑situ precipitation of a fine, ductile secondary phase along grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: Under operational conditions where the alloy is exposed to applied magnetic and pressure fields near its caloric phase transition and subjected to compressive or cyclic mechanical loads.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of fine, ductile precipitates at grain boundaries, which reinforce intergranular cohesion and arrest crack propagation.
generation.mechanism: The precipitates, generated by thermal treatment, improve load transfer at the grain boundaries and act as crack stoppers. They are engineered to have minimal impact on the crystallographic and magnetic/magnetocaloric structure that governs the caloric response.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated alloy, the heat‐treated material is expected to show a notable improvement in mechanical integrity (e.g., higher compressive strength and reduced crack formation) while maintaining a caloric response magnitude within acceptable experimental tolerance.
generation.baseline: The baseline is the undoped, conventionally processed (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy that shows high caloric performance but suffers from mechanical cracking under load.
generation.boundary: This intervention should be effective under the temperature, field, and pressure regimes that trigger the caloric effect. It assumes that annealing parameters are precisely controlled so that precipitate size and distribution are optimal; over-annealing or insufficient treatment may lead to either coarsening of precipitates or incomplete precipitation, potentially affecting either mechanical or caloric performance.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimization window for the annealing temperature and time is uncertain and requires experimental tuning to balance improved mechanical integrity with the preservation of caloric properties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy samples, one processed conventionally (baseline) and the other subjected to the tailored annealing treatment. Characterize the microstructure using electron microscopy to assess the precipitation of the ductile phase at grain boundaries. Then, perform compressive mechanical tests and calorimetric measurements under identical applied magnetic and pressure fields.
measurements: Electron microscopy (SEM/TEM) for precipitate size, distribution, and coherence at grain boundaries
Compressive strength and fracture toughness assessments
Caloric effect measurements (e.g., adiabatic temperature change or isothermal entropy change under field/pressure cycling)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the annealed samples fail to demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in mechanical integrity (e.g., higher compressive strength and reduced cracking) or if the caloric response is degraded by more than an acceptable margin relative to the untreated alloy.

cited_evidence.text: The microstructure, Vickers hardness, and compressive properties of novel low-activation VCrFeTaxWx (x = 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, and 1) high-entropy alloys (HEAs) were studied. The alloys were fabricated by vacuum-arc melting and the characteristics of these alloys were explored. The microstructures of all the alloys exhibited a typical morphology of dendritic and eutectic structures. The VCrFeTa0.1W0.1 and VCrFeTa0.2W0.2 alloys are essentially single phase, consisting of a disordered body-centered-cubic (BCC) phase, whereas the VCrFeTa0.2W0.2 alloy contains fine, nanoscale precipitates distributed in the BCC matrix. The lattice parameters and compositions of the identified phases were investigated. The alloys have Vickers hardness values ranging from 546 HV0.2 to 1135 HV0.2 with the x ranging from 0.1 to 1, respectively. The VCrFeTa0.1W0.1 and VCrFeTa0.2W0.2 alloys exhibit compressive yield strengths of 1341 MPa and 1742 MPa, with compressive plastic strains of 42.2% and 35.7%, respectively. VCrFeTa0.1W0.1 and VCrFeTa0.2W0.2 alloys have excellent hardness after annealing for 25 h at 600–1000 °C, and presented compressive yield strength exceeding 1000 MPa with excellent heat-softening

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing a low-volume (around 5–10 vol%) ductile, rare‐earth–free Cu-rich phase as an in situ precipitate will toughen the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy without significantly sacrificing its large caloric response.
drafts.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy exhibiting a large caloric effect but prone to cracking and poor mechanical integrity.
drafts.intervention: Implement a thermal processing route that promotes the in situ precipitation of a fine, ductile Cu-rich phase within the alloy matrix.
drafts.conditions: Under applied-field and pressure-field conditions, with temperature cycling near the alloy’s caloric phase transition and mechanical loading regimes similar to those used in previous compressive strength tests.
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation of coherent or semi-coherent Cu-rich precipitates that are uniformly dispersed, acting to arrest and deflect crack propagation at grain or phase boundaries.
drafts.mechanism: The dispersed ductile precipitates absorb and redistribute local stresses during loading, thereby increasing the overall compressive strength and integrity of the material. Because the Cu-rich phase is chosen to be non-disruptive with respect to the thermally driven phase transitions, the caloric effects are maintained within an acceptable margin.
drafts.predicted_outcome: An increase in compressive strength, ideally above 250 MPa (a relative increase of approximately 20–30% over the best epoxy-containing baseline), while reducing crack propagation; the caloric response (adiabatic temperature change and isothermal entropy change) is expected to remain within 5% of the baseline performance.
drafts.baseline: The original (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy with high caloric performance but compromised integrity, with compressive strengths under alternative composite routes ranging from 48 MPa (with low-melting In) to 218 MPa (with epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe).
drafts.boundary: This improvement is expected under typical operating field strengths and temperatures near the phase transition. The hypothesis applies when the volume fraction of the Cu-rich phase is kept low (5–10 vol%) and processing parameters are tuned to avoid coarsening of the precipitates, which could otherwise interfere with the caloric phase transition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the base (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy and another set with an optimized thermal treatment to induce a 5–10 vol% Cu-rich precipitate dispersion. Test both sets under identical conditions. Use mechanical testing (compressive strength tests) and measure the caloric effect (using techniques such as direct adiabatic temperature change measurement or latent heat characterization) under applied-field and pressure-field cycling.
measurements: Adiabatic temperature change (ΔT) under applied field cycles
Isothermal entropy change (ΔS) or latent heat associated with the phase transition
Microstructural characterization (e.g., SEM/TEM) to confirm the precipitate size, distribution, and coherence
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the Cu-modified samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase (at least 20% improvement) in compressive strength compared to the baseline, or if the caloric response (ΔT or ΔS/latent heat) degrades by more than approximately 5% relative to the base alloy under identical operating conditions.

drafts.hypothesis: A controlled heat‐treatment that induces in‐situ precipitation of a fine, ductile secondary phase along grain boundaries can simultaneously boost the mechanical integrity of the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high‐entropy alloy while preserving its high caloric performance under field and pressure cycling.
drafts.material_initial_state: The as-cast or conventionally processed (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy exhibits a coarse microstructure with mechanically weak grain boundaries leading to cracking, despite its large caloric response.
drafts.intervention: Apply a tailored annealing protocol at a controlled temperature (below the melting point of the primary phase but high enough for sufficient atomic mobility) to promote the precipitation of a uniformly distributed ductile secondary phase (e.g., a Mn-rich or Ni-rich phase) along the grain boundaries.
drafts.conditions: The intervention is designed for use under operational conditions where the alloy is exposed to applied magnetic and pressure fields near its caloric phase transition temperature, and under compressive loading representative of expected service stresses.
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation of fine, ductile precipitates at grain boundaries increases cohesion and acts as a crack-arresting mechanism, thereby toughening the overall microstructure.
drafts.mechanism: By precipitating a ductile phase in situ, the modified microstructure improves load transfer at the grain boundaries and resists crack propagation. The intervention is optimized such that the main crystallographic and magnetic structure responsible for the caloric effect remains largely unchanged.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated alloy, the heat-treated alloy is predicted to exhibit a significant increase in compressive strength (i.e. reduced cracking and improved integrity) with a negligible change or minimal shift (within acceptable tolerance) in the caloric response magnitude during field and pressure cycling.
drafts.baseline: The unmodified (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy, which demonstrates a robust caloric effect but poor mechanical integrity, prone to cracking under compressive loading.
drafts.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective under the temperature, field, and pressure regimes used to activate the caloric effect. It assumes that the annealing conditions are carefully optimized; excessive or insufficient annealing could result in overgrowth of precipitates or incomplete precipitation, respectively, potentially compromising either mechanical or caloric performance.

Characterize both sets using electron microscopy (SEM/TEM) to assess the microstructural evolution at grain boundaries. Then, conduct mechanical testing (e.g., compressive strength tests) and calorimetric measurements under applied magnetic and pressure fields to compare performance.
measurements: Microstructural characterization for precipitate size and distribution (SEM/TEM)
Compressive strength and fracture toughness measurements
Caloric effect magnitude (e.g., entropy change or temperature change under field/pressure cycling) using calorimetry
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in mechanical integrity (e.g., higher compressive strength and reduced cracking) or if the caloric response is significantly degraded compared to the untreated alloy, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: A minor compositional modification by adding a small amount of a high‐melting, ductile element (e.g. ~1–3 at.% Nb) to the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy will promote an in‑situ formation of a finely dispersed, ductile Nb‑rich BCC phase at grain boundaries. This second phase is expected to arrest crack initiation and propagation, thereby improving mechanical integrity without appreciably altering the caloric phase transformation responsible for the large caloric response.
drafts.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high‑entropy alloy that shows an excellent field‐induced caloric response but suffers from poor structural integrity (cracking under load).
drafts.intervention: Introduce a minor Nb addition (around 1–3 atomic percent) into the alloy composition during melting/annealing to encourage the precipitation of a ductile Nb‑rich phase along grain boundaries.
drafts.conditions: Under field‐cycling conditions (both applied magnetic field and pressure field) and standard thermal and mechanical loading (room temperature to moderate elevated temperatures) similar to those used to measure the caloric response.
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation of a finely dispersed, intergranular Nb‑rich ductile BCC phase that coexists with the parent caloric phase.
drafts.mechanism: The ductile phase serves as a built‑in binder that improves crack resistance and overall compressive/tensile integrity by arresting crack propagation at grain boundaries. Because the volume fraction is kept low, the transformation mechanisms responsible for the caloric effect in the main phase are minimally disturbed.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy should exhibit an increase in mechanical robustness (e.g. compressive yield strength and resistance to crack formation improved relative to, say, the 152–218 MPa benchmarks observed in epoxy‐containing systems) while retaining a caloric response similar in magnitude to the original alloy.
drafts.baseline: The undoped (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy, which shows large caloric response but low integrity due to its propensity to crack.
drafts.boundary: This approach is expected to work provided the Nb content remains low (≤3 at.%), and the thermal/annealing process is controlled so that the ductile phase precipitates finely without coarsening. Excessive Nb or overly aggressive processing may disrupt the caloric phase balance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloys with 0, 1, 2, and 3 at.% Nb added. Process the alloys under identical melting and annealing conditions that are known to yield the original caloric phase. Characterize the microstructure to confirm the presence, distribution, and size of any Nb‑rich phase. Then, subject specimens to both mechanical tests (e.g., compressive and fracture toughness measurements) and caloric measurements (under applied-field and pressure-field cycling) to assess changes in mechanical integrity and caloric response.
measurements: Microstructural analysis via TEM/SEM to verify ductile phase precipitation
Compressive and tensile tests to determine strength and crack resistance
Calorimetric studies (e.g., field-cycled differential scanning calorimetry) to quantify the entropy change/caloric effect
Comparative analysis against the undoped baseline alloy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-modified alloys do not show a statistically significant improvement in mechanical integrity (such as increased compressive yield strength and reduced cracking) or if the caloric response is reduced by more than approximately 10% compared to the undoped alloy, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Rapid solidification of the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy—via melt spinning or a similar high-cooling-rate process—will refine the microstructure (reducing grain size and homogenizing phase distribution) to suppress crack initiation and propagation while retaining the intrinsic caloric phase transformation, thereby improving mechanical integrity without sacrificing the large applied‐field/pressure-field caloric response.
drafts.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 produced by conventional casting, which shows a coarse microstructure with pronounced cracking under mechanical loading despite its high caloric performance.
drafts.intervention: Apply a rapid solidification processing route (e.g., melt spinning followed by controlled consolidation) to induce a fine-grained microstructure and a more uniform phase distribution.
drafts.conditions: Under working conditions where the alloy is subjected to applied magnetic or pressure fields at temperatures near the caloric effect transition (e.g., room temperature to moderately elevated temperatures) and under mechanical compressive/tensile loads typical for the intended actuator or refrigeration applications.
drafts.structural_mediator: A significantly refined grain structure with a high density of grain boundaries that act as barriers to crack nucleation and propagation, while preserving the phase responsible for the caloric effect.
drafts.mechanism: The rapid cooling minimizes segregation and reduces grain size, leading to enhanced toughness (via grain-boundary strengthening and crack deflection) without altering the intrinsic magneto/pressure-induced phase transformation that drives the caloric response.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Improved mechanical integrity (e.g., higher compressive/tensile strength and ductility, with reduced cracking) compared to the conventionally processed alloy, while maintaining nearly the same magnitude of caloric response (entropy or temperature change under field/pressure) within experimental tolerances.
drafts.baseline: Properties of the conventionally cast (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy, which exhibits high caloric performance but poor mechanical integrity (e.g., compressive strengths similar to 48–218 MPa in composite trials with epoxy or In, with frequent cracking).
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold when the cooling rate is sufficiently high to induce microstructural refinement but not so high as to induce an amorphous structure or unwanted compositional deviations; the operating temperature and loading regimes must remain within limits where the caloric phase transformation remains active.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 samples: one by conventional casting and one by rapid solidification (e.g., melt spinning followed by consolidation). Characterize the microstructure via SEM/TEM for grain size and phase uniformity; perform mechanical testing (compressive and tensile tests) to assess integrity (strength, ductility, crack initiation) and evaluate the caloric response (e.g., measure adiabatic temperature change or isothermal entropy change under applied fields or pressures). Compare both sets under identical operational conditions.
measurements: Grain size distribution and phase homogeneity (SEM/TEM)
Mechanical properties (compressive/tensile strength, ductility, crack propagation behavior)
Caloric performance metrics (temperature change and/or entropy change under applied field/pressure)
Thermal conductivity if relevant for heat transport
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the rapid solidification processed samples do not show a significant improvement in mechanical integrity (e.g., if strength or ductility are not statistically higher or cracking is not suppressed) or if the caloric response is reduced by more than a small acceptable margin (for instance >10% relative to the conventional cast material), then the hypothesis is falsified.
